feedback: Full understanding: gives 6/8/0 correctly AND explains the worm moves by squeezing and stretching with no legs, and transfers the idea to a new case such as the snail.
Partial: counts 6/8/0 correctly but lists them as separate facts — prompt 'how does the worm actually move with no legs?' to build the connection.

Gap: gives the same number for all three or insists the worm has tiny hidden legs — put a real or large-photo ant and spider side by side and count together, and watch a real worm move to show legless motion.
activities.intendedInsight: Leg number and way of moving are connected, not memorised as separate facts; some creatures move with no legs at all, and different legless creatures (worm vs snail) can move differently.
learnerActions: Look at an ant, a spider, and an earthworm. Say how many legs each one has (6, 8, and 0).
Explain how the one with no legs gets around — the worm squeezes and stretches its body, its muscles pushing it along and tiny bristles gripping the soil.
Extend to a new case: predict whether a snail has legs and how it moves (it has no legs and glides on a muscular foot over slime — a different legless mechanism from the worm).
Consider a probe: 'A centipede — would you expect 6 legs, 8, or lots more? Why?' and 'If something has 6 legs, what might it be?'
activities.title: Three minibeasts: count and explain (diagnostic)
